To help achieve this, the Customer Experience Improvement (CXI) team, within Amazon Customer Service (CS), relentlessly focuses on maintaining customer trust by building products that offer appropriate resolutions to resolve issues faced by our customers. CXI engineers solve complex problems and build scalable, robust solutions to help our customers navigate through issues and eliminate systemic defects to prevent future issues and identify critical customer experience improvement opportunities. Key job responsibilities
- Design, develop, and own scalable solutions that empower Amazon to deliver a defect-free experience for customers.
- Build intuitive tools for Customer Service Associates (CSAs) to escalate critical issues, and develop complex integrations with Tier-1 Amazon systems and advanced science models to detect, triage, and resolve systemic defects.
- Tackle complex technical challenges, create innovative solutions with direct impact on customer trust, and work on systems critical to Amazon's operational excellence.
About the team
ARCADE (Automated Root Causing, Attribution and Defect Elimination) is the Defect Elimination system within CXI Tech, manifesting Amazon's commitment to preventing customers from receiving defective products that degrade their experience. ARCADE leverages AI to transform how we detect repeat negative customer experiences and eliminate the underlying upstream defects at scale. The CXI Tech team re-imagines how we leverage customer interactions and feedback — through modular capabilities spanning Detection, Triage, Root Cause, Attribution, and Resolution — to enable more reliable and faster defect elimination that drives customer experience improvements throughout the consumer business. Join a team that builds the experiences every AWS customer uses to understand, monitor, and optimize what they spend, from individual developers to enterprise FinOps teams managing tens of millions of dollars in monthly spend. The AWS Billing Console Platform team owns the console's hosting platform, on which around thirty AWS engineering teams build their console pages; over fifty customer-facing billing and cost pages of its own; and the rendering engine that turns an AI agent's cost data into the charts, tables and reports customers see.
Two AWS agents answer cost questions today, a FinOps agent and Amazon Q in the console, and chatbots and console pages form one ecosystem customers navigate between to get problems solved and questions answered. Today each renders its answers its own way, and a cost figure has to be right the first time. This team is building the rendering layer both agents will draw on: an engine that checks every plotted value against the data the agent gathered, an open artifact format any agent host can render, and the component catalog that makes a cost chart look the same wherever it appears.
We are hiring a Software Development Engineer to extend this rendering platform to provide effective visualization for any problem that our web pages handle, especially for risky mutative actions. You'll use only the latest genAI, open source and proprietary technologies to directly enhance agents to give them the power of our AWS management console pages for problems that can only be solved visually or that require supervision by users.
Key job responsibilities
- Design, build, test, and operate the rendering engine behind AWS's cost agents: the components, the emit path, and the checks that verify every number before a customer sees it.
- Bring generated cost visualizations into agent conversations against the accuracy and customer-outcome bars the team sets, and keep two agent hosts rendering the same artifact from the same data.
- Define and publish a rendering format for cost artifacts and adopt the open protocol the console ecosystem is converging on.
- Build and operate customer-facing console pages on the team's page-building platform and component library.
- Help scale a platform that absorbed the work of three teams in a 2026 reorganization: drive down operational load through automation, observability, and legacy-service decommissioning so the team can invest in new customer experiences.

Midday you review a teammate's component, then join a design review where the team and the agent teams weigh how one artifact renders in two hosts. In the afternoon you pair with an applied scientist on the evaluation set for the next release and sketch the components a new chart needs. Across the week you balance net-new rendering and platform work against the operational excellence that billing customers depend on, and rotate through on-call. The problems are open-ended, the customer scale is large, and the design space is new, so there is room to set technical direction and take on new scope. Description
Annapurna Labs builds the custom silicon at the heart of AWS machine learning servers, and we are hiring a software engineer to help build the Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) that brings these chips to life. If you love working where hardware meets software, writing the code that boots, configures, and debugs some of the largest custom silicon in the world, this is your team.
As a Software Engineer on the SoC HAL team, you will write and test C++ for the driver stack across the hardware blocks that make up our chips, learn how the silicon works from the engineers who design it, and grow your skills on a small, fast-moving team inside a large organization. No machine learning background is required (you will pick up ML concepts from colleagues if you want to). This role is based in Cupertino, CA.
Key job responsibilities
Implement, test, and maintain HAL/driver features for individual hardware blocks (for example PCIe, DDR / HBM memory, DMA, system fabric, interrupt controllers, and boot / firmware), working from designs and interfaces set by more senior engineers.
Write clean, well-tested C++ and contribute to the team's test, code-review, and continuous-deployment practices.
Debug failures that span software and silicon, with support from the team, and build an understanding of how the HAL interacts with the hardware underneath it.
Learn the hardware/software interface by partnering with RTL and design verification engineers on well-scoped questions.
Provide feature additions and bug fixes on current and prior chips.
A day in the life
A typical day moves between writing and reviewing C++ for the HAL, pairing with a teammate on a tricky bug, and learning how a hardware block works from its spec or from the engineer who designed it. You might add a feature to a driver, write tests for it, and work through code-review feedback, then dig into a failure that spans software and silicon. Your teammates are the HAL engineers you build alongside; the hardware design, verification, and firmware teams are close partners you will learn from; and your customers are the internal software teams that rely on the HAL to boot, configure, and debug the chip.
About the team
Annapurna Labs designs and deploys some of the largest custom silicon in the world, including the Trainium and Inferentia machine learning accelerators. Our SoC HAL team builds the low-level software that boots, configures, and manages these chips, sitting between the hardware and the system software that runs the server. We are a small team that works closely with hardware, holds a high engineering bar, and invests in helping engineers grow. Based in Cupertino, CA, we value mentorship, clear written design, and software that outlasts any single chip.
Minimum Qualifications
- Knowledge of programming languages such as C/C++, Python, Java or Perl
- Experience (non-internship) in professional software development, or currently enrolled in or recently completed a Bachelor's or Master's degree in computer science or a related field
- Experience with data structures, algorithms, and software design fundamentals
Preferred Qualifications
- Bachelor's degree or above in Computer Science, Computer Engineering, or related fields at time of application
- Coursework, internship, or project experience in computer architecture or operating systems
- Experience with C or C++ and object-oriented design
- Exposure to low-level, embedded, or hardware-adjacent programming
